title: Is birth order important?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether birth order affects personality. They cover pop-psychology birth order traits (firstborn, middle, youngest, only child), the idea of a finite parental attention pie, and how blended families, big age gaps, twins, and adoption complicate the picture. They review science: studies disagree, confounding variables make results hard to isolate, and the Big Five personality inventory is discussed. They cover Alfred Adler's individual psychology, Frank Sulloway's Born to Rebel and the link between later-born children and revolutionary thinking, and the confluence model. A major section covers the fraternal birth order effect (more older brothers linked to higher odds of a boy being gay), the handedness finding, and the maternal immune hypothesis. The episode ends with a listener mail message from Sam and a brief tangent on the Motley Crue movie.

segments.title: Opening banter and birth order premise
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about their own birth orders, Josh noting he is the youngest of three. They introduce the idea that birth order may shape personality, and that it is hard to isolate among many other factors.

segments.title: Pop psychology birth order traits and parental attention
segments.summary: They outline the popular traits for firstborns, middle children, youngest children and only children. The theory is that parental attention and resources are a finite pie divided among more children. They also cover how firstborns are seen as conscientious and high achieving, and middles as people pleasers and peacemakers.

segments.title: Blended families, age gaps, twins and adoption
segments.summary: They discuss how blended families can displace a firstborn, and that personality is largely set by around age five, so younger children adapt more easily. They explain that a gap of five or more years can reset birth order, that twins act like firstborn or baby toward each other, and that adoption follows similar rules depending on the child's age.

segments.title: Science skepticism and confounding variables
segments.summary: They explain that scientific studies disagree on whether birth order effects exist, and that effects may be small compared with factors like socioeconomic status, race and gender. They describe how confounding variables such as demographic shifts and smoking prevalence can distort results.

segments.title: Alfred Adler and early birth order theory
segments.summary: They cover Alfred Adler, a contemporary of Freud who was among the first to discuss birth order and founded individual psychology. Adlerian therapy centers on a person's perceived power and position in the family and world, and birth order fits that framework through relative superiority or inferiority among siblings.

segments.title: Born to Rebel and Frank Sulloway's research
segments.summary: They discuss Frank Sulloway's book Born to Rebel, in which he argues firstborns tend to support the status quo while later-borns support revolutionary scientific ideas, with later-borns more likely to back Darwinism. They cover his explanations, including primogeniture, and the critique that his historical analysis is difficult. They also mention a Norwegian study finding a 2.3 IQ point difference between first and second-born children, which they find too small to be meaningful.

segments.title: Family reunions and personality as learned behavior
segments.summary: Josh describes how he falls back into the baby role around his family, and they discuss whether personality is learned and reinforced behavior that can be unlearned. They also share a story about the birthday dinner check.

segments.title: Fraternal birth order effect and sexual orientation
segments.summary: They discuss the fraternal birth order effect, in which each additional older brother is associated with a higher chance that a boy is gay. They note a cited figure of a 33 percent increase per older brother and a meta-analysis, and mention a British study that did not find the effect. They explain the social-pressure hypothesis.

segments.title: Handedness and maternal immune hypothesis
segments.summary: They report that the fraternal birth order effect appears only in right-handed men, with no difference among left-handed men. They describe a proposed biological explanation in which the mother's immune system reacts to male proteins with each successive male pregnancy, possibly affecting the development of later sons.

segments.title: Confluence model and tutor effect
segments.summary: They describe the confluence model, which says that adding younger siblings dilutes the emotional and intellectual environment of older children, and the tutor effect, in which a younger sibling can surpass an older one. The discussion then drifts into a tangent about The Police, Stewart Copeland, Sting, Les Claypool and The Residents.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sam and Motley Crue movie chat
segments.summary: Before the mail, Josh and Chuck discuss the Motley Crue movie on Netflix. Then they read a listener email from Sam, who thanks the hosts for support through his father's death, a breakup, and depression and anxiety.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite them to get in touch through the website or email, and close the episode.
